props.title: Starsky & Hutch
props.initialSlug: They don't make bad cops like they used to.

sections.content: Ben Stiller and Owen Wilson's chemistry drives this affectionate spoof of 1970s cop shows, particularly the original Starsky & Hutch (2004) TV series (1975-1979). Director Todd Phillips, fresh off Old School (2003), perfectly balances nostalgia and modern comedy, letting Stiller's uptight Starsky and Wilson's laid-back Hutch riff on the buddy cop dynamic that influenced everything from 48 Hrs. (1982) to Bad Boys (1995). Snoop Dogg's inspired casting as informant Huggy Bear adds authentic '70s swagger.

sections.content: The 2000s saw a wave of self-aware TV adaptations mining nostalgia for comedy gold. While Starsky & Hutch played it relatively straight, Charlie's Angels (2000) amped up the camp, and Land of the Lost (2009) went full parody. These films understood their source material's appeal while acknowledging changing audience expectations. The Brady Bunch Movie (1995) had earlier perfected this formula, dropping its 1970s characters unchanged into modern times for maximum culture clash comedy.

What sets Starsky & Hutch apart is its commitment to period detail - from the iconic red Ford Gran Torino to the pitch-perfect costume design. Unlike the broader comedy of Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery (1997), Phillips keeps the film grounded in character-driven humor while sneaking in clever commentary on masculinity and partnership, themes that defined the original series and 1970s cop shows like S.W.A.T. (1975) and Streets of San Francisco (1972-1977). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Buddy Cop Comedy

sections.content: The success of Starsky & Hutch influenced later buddy comedies like The Nice Guys (2016) and Central Intelligence (2016), proving audiences still crave the classic partnership dynamic. The film's careful balance of action and comedy follows a tradition established by Lethal Weapon (1987) and perfected by Bad Boys (1995), while adding its own self-aware twist. Even serious police dramas like End of Watch (2012) owe something to the partnership template Starsky & Hutch helped establish.
